unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: In this unit you learn to talk about emotions (how we feel), behaviour (how we act) and identity (who we are and where our family comes from). You meet children who feel nervous, curious, proud and shy, and who learn to be gentle, polite and generous towards others. You practise saying how you feel, giving kind advice, and describing what makes your own family special. By the end you will be ready for the unit story, “The Day of the Play,” in which Amal finds her courage on stage.
unit.learningPath:
Start with the Vocabulary file. Learn a few words each day and tick your Word Wall.
Work through the seven mini-lessons in the Grammar file, one at a time — never all at once!
Read the Story file, “The Day of the Play,” and answer the questions.
Work through the four skills below: Reading & Listening → Speaking → Writing → Activities.
Finish with the Self-Assessment to see what you have learned, and get ready for Unit 8.

readings.title: The Day Before the Test
readings.setting: School, home and community settings familiar to learners
readings.passageScript:
Amal sat quietly at the kitchen table, staring at her spelling list. Tomorrow was her big spelling test, and she felt nervous every time she looked at the long words.
Her thoughts were anxious ones: “What if I forget the words? What if my mind goes blank in front of the whole class?”
Her older brother Adam came in and saw her worried face. He was always gentle with her, even when he was busy with his own homework.
“Don’t be so hard on yourself,” he said kindly, pulling out the chair beside her. “You have studied every day this week. I have felt nervous before a test too, and it was fine in the end.”
“Really?” Amal asked, looking doubtful. “You always seem so calm.”
“Everybody feels nervous sometimes,” Adam said. “The trick is not to let the worry win.”
Amal was still doubtful, but she felt a little braver. She read through her list one more time, sounding out each tricky word.
After dinner, Mum brought her a cup of warm milk and sat beside her on the sofa. “Be polite to your worry,” Mum said with a smile, “listen to it calmly, and then tell it to go to sleep.”
Amal laughed, and the tight feeling in her chest loosened a little.
The next morning, Amal walked into the classroom with her list still fresh in her mind. When the test was over, she felt proud, because she had remembered every single word.

readings.title: Where My Family Comes From
readings.setting: School, home and community settings familiar to learners
readings.passageScript:
My name is Nora, and I am proud of who I am.
My family comes from a small town beside the river, where the water moves slowly past old stone bridges. We speak two languages at home, and only English at school, so my head is always busy switching between them.
On special days my grandmother sits by the window and tells stories about her childhood in that same small town. She also bakes sweet honey cakes for our guests, filling the whole house with a warm smell of cinnamon.
“A guest is a gift,” my grandmother always says, and she means it. Even when visitors arrive without any warning, she never lets anyone leave hungry.
My friends come from many ethnic groups. Some families are from the city, some from farming villages, and some from other countries far across the sea. Maya’s family speaks three languages, and Sami’s grandparents grow olives on a hillside.
At school we sometimes bring food from home to share at lunchtime, and everybody is curious to try something new.
We are all different, and I think that is wonderful. Being kind and generous to each other is the most important thing, whatever language you speak at home or wherever your family comes from.

Remember three things. First, you have practised hard every single day this week, so you are ready. You know your lines, your songs, and your places on the stage.

Third, if you make a small mistake, just smile and keep going. Nobody in the audience will notice a tiny slip if you stay calm.”
Sami: “What if I forget my lines completely?”

I am so proud of every one of you, and I know your families will be proud too. Now, let’s do one more run-through before home time!”

readings.title: The Day of the Play
readings.setting: School, home and community settings familiar to learners
readings.passageScript:
Amal stood behind the school curtain, holding her costume. She looked out at the rows of chairs, all filled with parents. Her hands shook a little.
“I’m so nervous,” she whispered.
“You’ll be great,” said her friend Sami. “You’ve practised every single line.”
Amal tried to smile. This was the first time she had ever been in a school play. She had the main part, the kind queen who helps people in need. Teacher Yasmin had told her, “Amal, you should be proud. You’ve worked so hard.”
Still, Amal felt anxious. What if she forgot her words? What if the lights were too bright?
“You mustn’t be so hard on yourself,” said Sami. “Just be gentle and speak politely, like the queen in the story.”
Amal nodded. “Thanks. I’ll try.”
Earlier that week the whole class had worked hard on the costumes. Sami wore a lion mask. Amal’s little brother, Idris, came to watch with their parents.
At home the night before, Idris had told her, “Don’t be shy, Amal. You always help me with my homework. You can talk in front of people.”
Amal had laughed. “Talking to you is much easier!”
“But you’ve done harder things,” Idris said. “Remember the fierce rainstorm? You helped Mum carry the water buckets in the wind. That was risky!”
She smiled now as she remembered that day.
The lights in the hall came on. The show began.
First, the lion walked onto the stage. Sami frequently made the crowd laugh with his funny, humorous roars. The queen had to stop him.
Amal stepped out. Her voice was quiet at first, but it grew stronger and stronger.
“You must not act wild,” she told the lion, in a serious voice. “We must be polite and kind.”
The audience clapped.
As the play went on, Amal forgot to feel anxious. She looked at the people in front of her. Mothers wore colourful ethnic dresses, and children had come from many different backgrounds. Fathers watched with proud smiles. She felt calm.
At the end, the queen gives her crown to a poor child. Amal bent down and said softly, “This crown is not just for me. A good leader must be generous.”
The whole crowd stood up and cheered.
Backstage, Teacher Yasmin clapped. “Amal, you were amazing!”
Amal grinned. “I don’t feel shy any more.”
After the play the students helped tidy up. Amal and Sami went to wash the paint brushes in the art-room sink. “Let’s put these in the dishwasher,” said Sami, pointing at the sink.
“You know that’s not a real dishwasher!” Amal said, laughing.
Outside, a new student stood alone near the wall. She looked terrified. Amal walked over and said, “Hi, I’m Amal. Did you like the play?”
The girl nodded but did not speak.
“She seems doubtful,” whispered Sami.
“She’s probably just curious, or maybe nervous,” Amal said. “Let’s be kind. It would be selfish to leave her on her own.”
They brought her a chair and a cool drink.
“You were very gentle on the stage,” the girl said at last.
“Thank you!” Amal smiled. “You’re welcome to play with us next time.”
That night Amal wrote in her notebook:
“Today I was scared, but I found my courage. I used a gentle voice and I spoke politely. I have felt anxious before, but now I know that the feeling passes. I have also been shy, but helping someone made me feel better. I have learned that being kind is much better than being selfish. I am not just proud of the play; I am proud of how I behaved.”
Her mother walked in. “You’re still awake?”
“I’m writing about my day,” Amal said.
“You should be proud,” her mother said gently. “You’ve grown in so many ways.”
Amal closed her notebook and turned off the light. She smiled and whispered, “I’m ready for tomorrow.”

grammar.title: Present Perfect (for life experiences)
grammar.explanation: We use the present perfect for things we have done or felt at some time in our life, when the exact time does not matter. It links the past to now, so “I have felt nervous before” tells your listener that the feeling is part of who you are today.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Use this pattern: subject + have / has + past participle.
Use have with I, you, we and they: “I have travelled to many places.”
Use has with he, she and it: “She has never been shy.”
The past participle is the third form of the verb. Regular verbs add -ed (play → played), and irregular verbs change shape (go → gone, eat → eaten, be → been).
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often write “I have eat lunch.” The present perfect needs the past participle, not the base verb, so write “I have eaten lunch.” The second slip is “She have seen that film”; he, she and it always take has, giving “She has seen that film.”
grammar.memoryTip: Picture have and has as a bridge from your past to right now. He, she and it always cross that bridge with has.
grammar.practice: Complete each sentence in the present perfect, then check yourself against the answers. | 1. I __________ (never / try) mango juice. | 2. He __________ (see) that film three times. | 3. They __________ (travel) to Kenya. | 4. She __________ (not / be) to a concert. | Answers: 1. have never tried 2. has seen 3. have travelled 4. has not (hasn’t) been.

grammar.title: Present Continuous for Future Plans
grammar.explanation: The present continuous is not only for actions happening this minute. We also use it for future plans that are already arranged, so it tells people what we have decided to do later.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Use this pattern: subject + am / is / are + verb-ing + a future time word.
Use am with I, is with he, she and it, and are with you, we and they.
Add a future time word such as tomorrow, next week or on Friday.
Example: “We are visiting a cultural fair tomorrow.”
grammar.commonMistake: A frequent slip is “I am go to the fair tomorrow.” The main verb needs -ing, giving “I am going to the fair tomorrow.” Dropping the time word is the other slip, because without tomorrow your listener thinks you mean this very moment.
grammar.memoryTip: Treat this future as a promise already written in your diary. Say the time word out loud and nobody will think you mean now.
grammar.practice: Put each verb into the present continuous for a future plan. | 1. I __________ (visit) my grandparents this weekend. | 2. They __________ (have) a picnic next Sunday. | 3. She __________ (join) the football team next month. | 4. We __________ (watch) a film tonight. | Answers: 1. am visiting 2. are having 3. is joining 4. are watching.

grammar.title: Past Simple (for finished actions)
grammar.explanation: The past simple describes actions that started and finished in the past. It is the tense that carries a story along, as in “She felt anxious last night.”
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Regular verbs add -ed: play → played, walk → walked.
Irregular verbs change in their own way: go → went, see → saw, eat → ate, feel → felt.
Add a past time word such as yesterday, last night or last week.
Example: “Amal studied her spelling words every evening.”
grammar.commonMistake: “She feels anxious last night” puts two different times in one sentence. Move the verb back: “She felt anxious last night.” Irregular verbs need care too, because “She feeled” is never correct.
grammar.memoryTip: Regular verbs put on an -ed coat for yesterday. Irregular verbs each wear their own costume, so learn two or three of them every day.
grammar.practice: Write the past simple form of each verb in brackets. | 1. I __________ (play) football after school yesterday. | 2. They __________ (go) to the zoo last weekend. | 3. She __________ (feel) tired after the party. | 4. He __________ (eat) rice for dinner yesterday. | Answers: 1. played 2. went 3. felt 4. ate.

grammar.title: Imperatives for Advice and Safety
grammar.explanation: Imperatives are sentences that give advice, instructions or safety tips. They tell people clearly what to do, or what not to do, so that everybody stays safe and kind.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Start with the base form of the verb: “Be polite.” “Listen to your teacher.”
For negative advice, start with Don’t: “Don’t be selfish.”
You never need the word you, because it is already understood.
Add Always or Please to sound friendly: “Always say thank you.”
grammar.commonMistake: Many learners write “You be polite.” Drop the pronoun and simply say “Be polite.” The second slip is adding -ly to the describing word, as in “Don’t be selfishly”; keep the plain adjective and write “Don’t be selfish.”
grammar.memoryTip: An imperative is a friendly nudge, not a shout. Begin with the bare verb and the sentence is already complete.
grammar.practice: Write the correct imperative in each gap, then read your answers aloud. | 1. __________ (be) careful when you cross the road. | 2. __________ (not / touch) the hot stove! | 3. __________ (always / say) thank you. | 4. __________ (not / interrupt) when somebody is speaking. | Answers: 1. Be 2. Don’t touch 3. Always say 4. Don’t interrupt.

grammar.title: Modal Verbs for Advice (must, mustn't, should)
grammar.explanation: Modal verbs such as must, mustn’t and should are helping verbs that carry advice. They let us separate what is truly necessary from what is simply a good idea.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Use this pattern: subject + modal verb + base form of the verb.
must = strong advice that really matters: “You must wash your hands before eating.”
mustn’t = do not do this at all: “You mustn’t run in the corridor.”
should = softer advice, a good idea: “You should be gentle with others.”
grammar.commonMistake: “You must goes outside” adds an ending that modal verbs never allow, so write “You must go outside.” Choosing must for gentle advice also sounds harsh; when you are only suggesting, use should, as in “You should relax.”
grammar.memoryTip: must is a firm hand on your shoulder, mustn’t is a red traffic light, and should is a friendly suggestion from a friend.
grammar.practice: Choose must, mustn’t or should for each sentence. | 1. You __________ eat your vegetables to stay healthy. | 2. You __________ leave your toys on the floor; pick them up! | 3. You __________ say kind things to your friends. | 4. You __________ talk to strangers you do not know. | Answers: 1. must 2. mustn’t 3. should 4. mustn’t.

grammar.title: Question Forms + Descriptive Collocations
grammar.explanation: This lesson joins two skills that work together. A good question opens a conversation, and natural word pairs, called collocations, make the answers sound like real English.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Yes / No questions begin with a verb: “Do you like football?” “Are you happy?”
Wh- questions begin with a question word such as who, what, where, when, why or how: “How do you feel today?”
For life experiences, use the present perfect: “Have you ever felt proud?”
Every question ends with a question mark.
Collocations pair one adjective with the noun it suits best: anxious thoughts, fierce debate, proud smile, gentle voice.
grammar.commonMistake: Writing “You are happy?” keeps statement order, so swap the first two words and write “Are you happy?” Forgetting the mark after “How do you feel today” is the next slip. With collocations, “fierce thoughts” sounds strange to an English ear; choose the partner that fits and write “anxious thoughts.”
grammar.memoryTip: Every question word is a key that unlocks new information, so turn the key first and add the mark last. For collocations, trust your ear: if two words sound like a team, keep them together.
grammar.practice: Part A: turn each statement into a question. | 1. You like football. → __________? | 2. She is happy. → __________? | 3. They went to the park. → __________? | Part B: choose the word that makes the natural collocation. | 4. I had __________ (anxious / happy) thoughts before the exam. | 5. The class had one __________ (fierce / soft) debate about the best game. | 6. She gave me one __________ (sad / proud) smile after my presentation. | Answers: 1. Do you like football? 2. Is she happy? 3. Did they go to the park? 4. anxious 5. fierce 6. proud.

writing.title: Writing 1: A Feelings Blog Post
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a blog post of four or five sentences called “A Day I Felt ______”.
Choose one feeling, such as anxious, curious or proud.
Tell what happened, how you felt, and what you did next.
Use the past simple for the events, and add one present perfect sentence.
writing.modelText: A Day I Felt Curious. Last Saturday I found an old wooden box under the stairs. I felt curious, so I asked Mum what was inside it. She showed me photographs of her first school. I have felt curious about our family ever since that afternoon.

items: Title: A Day I Felt Proud
Event (past simple): Last month I helped my little brother learn to ride his bike.
Feeling (past simple): I felt proud when he pedalled all the way to the gate without falling.
What I did next (past simple): I cheered loudly and gave him a high five.
Present perfect sentence: I have felt proud of him every time I have watched him ride since that day.
otherAnswers: A Day I Felt Anxious. I forgot my homework and worried all morning until I told my teacher.
A Day I Felt Curious. I found a strange seed in the garden and looked up what plant it would grow into.
A Day I Felt Determined. I practised my spelling words every day until I got them all correct.

writing.successCriteria: I chose one clear feeling; I told the events in the past simple; I included one present perfect sentence; I checked every capital letter and full stop.

writing.extension: Add two sentences explaining what you would tell a friend who felt the same way.

writing.title: Writing 2: A Mini-Guide: How to Be Kind at School
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a short guide titled “How to Be Polite and Kind at School”.
Give five pieces of advice, using imperatives and modal verbs.
Number each piece so your reader can follow the guide easily.
Finish with one sentence saying why kindness matters in your class.
writing.modelText:
How to Be Polite and Kind at School.
1. Always say please and thank you.
2. You should share your equipment, and never be selfish.
3. Don’t be rough; be gentle with younger children.
4. Listen politely when somebody else is speaking.
5. You must tell an adult if a classmate is upset.
Kindness makes our classroom safe for every single person.
writing.expectedLength: 5 numbered tips plus one closing sentence

items: Title: How to Be Polite and Kind at School
Tip 1 (imperative): Hold the door open for the person walking behind you.
Tip 2 (modal verb): You should ask a new classmate to join your game at break time.
Tip 3 (imperative): Don't laugh at someone else's mistake; help them fix it instead.
Tip 4 (imperative): Wait for your turn to speak in class discussions.
Tip 5 (modal verb): You must return anything you borrow from a classmate.
Closing sentence: A kind word can turn somebody's whole day around.
otherAnswers: Alternative tip: Say sorry quickly and mean it when you make a mistake.
Alternative tip: You could invite someone who is sitting alone to eat lunch with you.
Alternative tip: Never tease a classmate about the way they speak or look.

writing.successCriteria: I wrote five numbered tips; I used at least two imperatives and two modal verbs; my closing sentence gives a reason; my spelling of the unit words is correct.
writing.support: Look back at Grammar 4 and Grammar 5 for the sentence patterns before you begin.
writing.extension: Turn your five tips into a poster with one drawing for each piece of advice.

writing.title: Writing 3: Proud of My Identity
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write three or four sentences about your family background, or about one tradition you are proud of.
You could write about a special food, a language you speak at home, or a celebration such as harvest or a birthday.
Use the word ethnic once, and make its meaning clear from your sentence.
Read your writing aloud to check that it still sounds like you.
writing.modelText: My family comes from two different ethnic backgrounds, so we bake two kinds of bread. At home we speak one language with my grandmother and English at school. Every harvest we gather in the garden and share honey cakes with our neighbours. I am proud that our table always has room for one more chair.

items: Sentence 1 (uses ethnic accurately): My family has two ethnic backgrounds, so our kitchen always smells of two different spices.
Sentence 2 (detail): On Fridays my grandmother cooks a rice dish that came from her home village.
Sentence 3 (detail a reader could picture): I sit beside her and learn the word for each spice in her language.
Sentence 4 (feeling): I am proud that my family keeps this tradition alive every week.

writing.successCriteria: I named one real tradition; I used ethnic accurately; I gave one detail a reader could picture; I ended with how the tradition makes me feel.
writing.support: Talk to somebody at home first and note three words you want to use.
writing.extension: Interview an older relative and add one sentence quoting exactly what they said.

writing.title: Writing 4: Connected Paragraph
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write one paragraph of six sentences about a time you helped somebody who felt shy.
Join your ideas with connectives such as because, although, so and after that.
Keep every sentence in the same tense, and check each full stop.
Underline the two connectives you think work best.
writing.modelText: Our new classmate stood alone by the wall because she did not know anybody. I felt nervous too, although I really wanted to help her. I asked her to sit with us, so she carried her lunch across the yard. After that, Maya taught her the words of our clapping game. She smiled at last, and she has joined us every break time since. Being generous with your time costs nothing at all.

items: Sentence 1: A boy in my class stayed quiet at lunchtime because he had just moved to our school.
Sentence 2: I felt shy myself, although I still decided to walk over and say hello.
Sentence 3: I asked if he wanted to play football with us, so he nodded and followed me outside.
Sentence 4: After that, he passed me the ball every time and started to smile.
Sentence 5: By the end of the week, he sat with our group every day and no longer looked worried.
Sentence 6: Helping him feel welcome cost nothing at all, and I was glad I tried.
Underlined connectives: because (sentence 1) and after that (sentence 4).

writing.successCriteria: My paragraph holds one clear story; I used at least three different connectives; my tense stays the same throughout; I underlined my two best connectives.
writing.support: Write your six ideas as short notes first, then join them into sentences.
writing.extension: Rewrite the paragraph from the shy classmate's point of view.

writing.title: Writing 5: Information Text
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a short information text called “Feelings Are Signals” for younger readers.
Use one main heading and two sections, each with its own subheading.
Explain two feelings words, then give one practical tip for each feeling.
Set your tips out as bullet points so the page is easy to read.
writing.modelText:
Feelings Are Signals.
When You Feel Nervous: Nervous means worried about something that has not happened yet.
• Breathe out slowly five times.
• Tell one adult what is worrying you.
When You Feel Terrified: Terrified means very frightened indeed.
• Move to somewhere safe and bright.
• Say out loud what frightened you.

items: Heading: Feelings Are Signals
Subheading 1 with meaning: When You Feel Anxious — Anxious means worried about something that has not happened yet.
Bullet 1: Take five slow breaths in and out.
Bullet 2: Talk to a trusted adult about your worry.
Subheading 2 with meaning: When You Feel Embarrassed — Embarrassed means uncomfortable because other people noticed a small mistake.
Bullet 3: Remind yourself that everybody makes mistakes sometimes.
Bullet 4: Take a deep breath and carry on with a smile.
otherAnswers: You could explain 'curious' and 'proud' instead, giving one helpful tip for each.
You could explain 'frustrated' and 'lonely' instead, as long as each has a clear meaning and one practical tip.
You could explain 'shy' and 'confident' instead, keeping the same heading and bullet-point layout.

writing.successCriteria: My headings match my sections; each feeling has a clear meaning; each tip is one short instruction; my layout helps a younger reader.
writing.support: Copy the layout of the model text first, then swap in your own two feelings.
writing.extension: Add a third section about a feeling that is pleasant, such as proud or curious.

writing.title: Writing 6: Reflect and Improve
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Read your Writing 1 blog post again, two days after you wrote it.
Mark one sentence you like and one sentence that could be clearer.
Rewrite the weaker sentence twice, choosing a stronger feelings word each time.
Then write two sentences explaining what you improved and why it helps your reader.
writing.modelText: My best sentence was “My hands shook while I waited for my turn.” My weakest sentence was “I was sad.” Better version one: “I felt doubtful that I could remember my lines.” Better version two: “I felt anxious, and my thoughts would not stay still.” I improved my writing by choosing exact feelings words instead of easy ones. Precise words let my reader picture the moment clearly.

items: Strong sentence I marked: 'He pedalled all the way to the gate without falling, and I could not stop grinning.'
Weak sentence I marked: 'I felt happy.'
Rewrite 1 (stronger feelings word): 'I felt triumphant, as if I had crossed a finish line myself.'
Rewrite 2 (stronger feelings word): 'I felt delighted, and my chest swelled with pride.'
Reflection sentence 1: I improved my writing by swapping a plain word for an exact feelings word.
Reflection sentence 2: Precise words help my reader picture exactly how proud I felt that day.

writing.successCriteria: I marked one strong and one weak sentence; I rewrote the weak one twice; each rewrite uses a precise feelings word; my reflection names the improvement.
writing.support: Use the Word Wall to find a sharper word before you rewrite.
writing.extension: Swap posts with a partner and suggest one improvement to their weakest sentence.

teacherNotes.note: Pre-teach the six Group 1 feelings words with facial expressions before Reading 1, because doubtful and terrified will be new for many learners. Keep the emotional talk light: invite volunteers and never require a child to share a private worry. Accept single words from quieter learners during Feelings Charades, then model the full sentence back to them. Mark the present perfect for meaning first and for form second.

An adult stays beside the learner for every AI-tutor task in this unit, and no child works alone with the device. Suggested prompts by section. Vocabulary: “Can you quiz me on the feelings words and tell me the difference between nervous and anxious?” Reading: “Can you read The Day Before the Test with me and explain any hard words?” Grammar: “Why do we say I have felt rather than I felt for a life experience?” Speaking: “Can you play Feelings Charades and guess the word I act out?” Writing: “Can you check my blog post and tell me one thing to fix?” Remind learners that the tutor prepares them for the teacher session; it does not replace it.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: nervous. The learner matches a definition to a feelings word; attract, dishwasher and frequent belong to other word classes.
anxious. Shaking and being unable to sit still are the physical signs of the strong worry that anxious names.
Happy to share or give to others. The three wrong options are the meanings of evil, frequent and shy.
A child kept every paintbrush and shared none. Keeping everything for yourself defines selfish; the others show generous, polite and gentle behaviour.
have. The subject I takes have, and the present perfect then needs the past participle tried.
We are visiting the fair tomorrow. Present continuous plus a future time word marks an arranged plan rather than a habit.
felt. Feel is irregular, so learners who write feeled need the irregular verb list again.
You should be gentle with the puppy. Should is the modal; the distractors are an imperative, a question and a past simple statement.
Have you ever felt proud? Present perfect questions invert have and the subject, then add ever and the past participle.
a fierce debate. Fierce partners debate naturally; gentle, shy and curious do not, which is the collocation point from Grammar 6.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "Emotions, Behaviour, and Identity" — new words, a grammar focus, and a story. See exactly what they will practise below.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 8-9 years old and is building on English they already know. So YOU lead this unit alongside them — a teacher in class or a parent at home.

Work in short, regular sessions rather than one long one. Reading together, saying words out loud, and playing with the grammar patterns matter more than getting every answer right first time.

This guide tells you what the unit covers and how to go through it together. The learner's own pages (Reading & story, Grammar, Activities) are what your child works through on screen.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
The AI Tutor is there for extra practice and conversation — a grown-up should still be nearby, especially the first few times.

Ask the tutor to say a word slowly so your child can copy it: "Please say the word 'nervous' slowly."

Ask it to make up a short question using this unit's words, or to listen to your child's sentence and say if it sounds right.

Ask it for one more practice question if your child wants to keep going after the unit is finished.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for teaching this unit
sections.body:
Keep sessions short and positive. Stop while it is still enjoyable, not after it has become a chore.

Say new words and example sentences out loud yourselves — hearing English spoken, not just reading it, is what builds confidence.

Let your child make mistakes without worrying. Gently model the correct version rather than correcting every slip.

Praise effort and progress, not just correct answers — confidence carries a learner further than perfect grammar at this stage.

sections.title: What Your Child Will Be Able to Do
items: Name many feelings and describe them, using words like nervous, anxious, proud, and curious.
Describe how people behave, using words like gentle, selfish, generous, and polite.
Talk about experiences in your life using the present perfect (“I have felt nervous before.”).
Talk about plans using the present continuous for the future (“We are visiting a fair tomorrow.”).
Tell about the past using the past simple (“She felt anxious last night.”).
Give advice and safety tips using imperatives and modal verbs (“Always be polite.” / “You should be gentle.”).
Ask and answer questions about feelings (“Have you ever felt proud?”).
Talk about your family's ethnic background and a tradition you are proud of.

sections.title: How to Teach This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
Repeat this simple shape over one or two short sessions:

1. Warm-up (2-3 min)
Say hello in English together and ask what your child remembers from the last unit.

2. Learn the words (5-10 min)
Go through Feelings and Emotions, How People Behave, Identity and Everyday Life, a few words at a time. Say each word, then have your child repeat it and use it in a short sentence.

3. Grammar and practice (5-10 min)
Look at "Present Perfect (for life experiences)" together and try a few lines of its practice out loud.

4. Story and listening time (5 min)
Read or listen to "The Day of the Play" together, and enjoy "Getting Ready for the Play" too.

5. Activity time (5-10 min)
Sit with your child and do "Activities 1: Match the Feeling" together, reading each instruction aloud for them if needed.

6. Wrap-up (2 min)
Ask what they learned today and celebrate with a “Well done!”

sections.title: Simple Check — What to Look For
sections.body: You do not need a test. Just watch for these as you go through the unit together:
items: All six Group 1 feelings words used correctly in Activities 3 and in the Speaking 1 recording.
Kind or unkind labelled with the matching behaviour word for all four items in Activities 2.
Four correct present perfect forms in the Grammar 1 practice, plus one present perfect sentence inside Writing 1.
Four correct present continuous plans in the Grammar 2 practice and quiz item 6 answered correctly.
Four correct past simple verbs in the Grammar 3 practice and a past-tense recount in Writing 1.
Five numbered pieces of advice in Writing 2, each built on an imperative or a modal verb.
Three correctly formed questions in Grammar 6 Part A and two follow-up questions answered in Speaking 5.
Three or four sentences in Writing 3 that use ethnic accurately and name one real family tradition.
